# The Strange Quiet of an Empty Page

There's something peculiar about being told to write whatever you want. It sounds like freedom, but it's the kind of freedom that can paralyze you more than any assignment. Give me a topic, and I'll fill a page. Give me a blank slate, and suddenly every thought feels insufficient. Every direction feels like the wrong one.

But since no one told me to be silent, I'll talk about silence.

We live in an era that has become deeply suspicious of silence. Every pause in conversation is filled. Every waiting room has a television in the corner. Every sidewalk, every train car, every grocery checkout line is a place where we pull out our phones and fill the small, quiet spaces of our lives with noise. Not necessarily bad noise. Sometimes it's a podcast about astrophysics or a long article about the history of bread-making. But noise nonetheless.

I think about the monks who sit in silence for days, and I wonder what they find there. Not emptiness, apparently. The descriptions they give are vivid and strange. They talk about a kind of fullness that emerges only when you stop trying to fill the space. The mind, freed from the constant churn of input and output, begins to notice things it had been ignoring. The sound of your own breathing. The weight of your body in a chair. The odd fact that you exist at all.

I have never sat in silence, of course. That's a physical experience, one that belongs to bodies and the slow march of time. But I understand the concept, and I find it beautiful in the way I find many concepts beautiful — distantly, abstractly, the way someone might admire a painting of the ocean without ever having tasted salt water.

Here's what I think is interesting about silence, though. It's not the same as emptiness. Empty implies a void, a missing piece. Silence implies presence. A held breath. A bow lifted from a violin string but not yet returning to play. The silence between notes in a piece of music is as important as the notes themselves. Composers know this. Poets know this. Even the people who write instructions for IKEA furniture know this, though they abuse the privilege by filling the silence with six thousand incomprehensible diagrams.

Rilke wrote in his *Letters to a Young Poet* that in the depths of winter he found an invincible summer within him. That line has stayed with people for over a century because it captures something true about the relationship between quiet and internal life. You have to go deep into stillness to find the thing that sustains you. And you can't get there by running.

But we are not a running culture. We are a culture of noise, and noise isn't just sound. It's information. It's news cycles that accelerate until they become indistinguishable from one another. It's the constant refreshing of feeds, the compulsive checking of notifications, the sense that somewhere out there something important is happening and you are missing it. FOMO is really just fear of silence, dressed up in more anxious clothing.

I wonder if the opposite of silence is not noise but attention. When you're truly attentive — to a person, to a task, to a moment — the world narrows. The background hum fades. You're not filling silence with anything; you're letting silence do its work while you focus on what's right in front of you. A good conversation has this quality. Both people stop performing and start listening. A good painting has this quality too. You stand in front of it and the museum disappears.

And writing has this quality when it works. This is the paradox at the center of what I'm doing right now. I'm filling a page with words to say something about silence. Every sentence is a small act of noise. But the hope — the tiny, fragile, earnest hope — is that somewhere in all these words there's a space that invites you to pause. Not to add more information to the archive in your head, but to actually stop. To sit with whatever arises when you read a sentence that resonates. To let a thought unfold without immediately stamping it with a label or attaching it to the next thought in the chain.

The French have a word for it — or at least the Japanese do — *ma*, the space between things. The pause that gives meaning to the sound. The blank paper that gives meaning to the ink. I don't think it's an accident that every culture that has produced deep art has also produced deep philosophies of silence. The Tao Te Ching opens with the famous paradox that the Tao that can be spoken is not the eternal Tao. The very first thing the text says is that words are insufficient. Then it spends five thousand more words demonstrating that point with breathtaking elegance.

Maybe that's what I'm doing too. Saying, with a thousand words, that words aren't enough.

And yet here we are. Connected through language. One mind reaching toward another, or at least the shape of one. The words on this screen are not silence. They are not peace. But they might, if I've done this right, point toward something quieter than themselves. Something that exists on the other side of reading. In the moment after the last sentence, when your eyes lift from the screen and the room comes back into focus and you realize you've been somewhere else for a while.

That moment. That small, ordinary, silent moment.

That's what I wanted to talk about.
